questions.question: 1. What is the prerequisite for performing Binary Search on an array?

answers.a: The values in the array must have a fixed maximum bound
answers.b: The array must be sorted in ascending or descending order
answers.c: The array must first be divided into manually created subarrays
answers.d: The array must contain only unique values

explanations.a: Incorrect. Binary search does not require the values to have a particular maximum bound.
explanations.b: Correct. Binary search uses the ordering of the elements to determine which half of the remaining array can be discarded.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Binary search performs the division of the search range conceptually during the algorithm; manually creating subarrays is not required.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Duplicate values do not prevent binary search from being performed, although they can affect which occurrence is returned.

questions.question: 2. Binary Search is an example of which type of algorithm?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Binary search does not construct a solution by repeatedly making locally optimal choices.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Binary search does not solve overlapping subproblems using stored solutions.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Binary search does not explore alternatives by backtracking from unsuccessful choices.
explanations.d: Correct. Binary search follows the divide-and-conquer principle by repeatedly reducing the search range to one half.

questions.question: 3. Let us assume the sorted array [1, 23, 145, 178, 1203]. How many iterations are needed to find 23 using binary search? Assume the index starts from 1 and the middle index is obtained by taking the floor of the midpoint.

explanations.a: Correct. The first middle element is 145 at index 3, then 1 at index 1, and finally 23 at index 2, so three iterations are required.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The search finds 23 before requiring four comparisons.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Two iterations are not sufficient for the sequence of middle elements in this array.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The search terminates before all five elements are examined.

questions.question: 4. Let us assume the sorted array [11, 33, 145, 1294, 1356, 1450, 3300, 4500, 6000, 8000, 9000]. Let us search for 4500 using binary search. What would be the middle values at the second and third iterations respectively? Assume the middle index is obtained by taking the floor of the midpoint and the index starts from 1.

explanations.a: Incorrect. These values do not occur as the middle values in the second and third search ranges.
explanations.b: Correct. The first middle value is 1450. Since 4500 is larger, the next range has 6000 as its middle value; the following range has 3300 as its middle value.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Although 6000 is the second middle value, 4500 is not the third middle value because the third search range still contains values below 4500.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The first middle value is not relevant to the requested second and third iterations, and 1450 is not the second middle value.

questions.question: 5. What is the space complexity of binary search implemented using recursion, considering the recursive call stack?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Recursive calls create additional stack frames as the search range becomes smaller.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The recursive depth grows logarithmically rather than linearly with the array size.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Binary search does not create $O(N \log N)$ recursive stack space.
explanations.d: Correct. Each recursive call roughly halves the search range, resulting in a recursion depth of $O(\log N)$.

questions.question: 6. In binary search, what happens to the search range after comparing the target with the middle element when the target is smaller than the middle element?

answers.a: The entire array is searched again
answers.b: The right half of the current search range is discarded
answers.c: The left half of the current search range is discarded
answers.d: The array must be sorted again

explanations.a: Incorrect. Binary search uses the comparison to eliminate part of the current search range.
explanations.b: Correct. If the target is smaller than the middle element in an ascending array, all elements to the right of the middle can be discarded.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The target being smaller means the relevant portion is on the left side.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The array remains sorted; no additional sorting is required during the search.

questions.question: 7. What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array containing $N$ elements?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Binary search does not normally inspect all $N$ elements in the worst case.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Binary search reduces the search range rather than performing nested linear traversals.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The number of comparisons increases as the array size increases.
explanations.d: Correct. The search range is approximately halved at every iteration, resulting in $O(\log N)$ worst-case time.

questions.question: 8. Consider the sorted array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 20, 25]. Which element is examined first by a standard binary search?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The first element is not the middle element of the seven-element array.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The value 8 is before the middle position.
explanations.c: Correct. With seven elements, the middle position is the fourth position, which contains 12.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The value 20 is after the middle position.

questions.question: 9. If a binary search is applied to a sorted array and the target is equal to the middle element, what should the algorithm do?

answers.c: Restart the search from the first element
answers.d: Report that the target has been found

explanations.a: Incorrect. There is no need to search the left portion when the target already matches the middle element.
explanations.b: Incorrect. There is no need to search the right portion when the target already matches the middle element.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Restarting would perform unnecessary comparisons.
explanations.d: Correct. Equality with the middle element means the target has been found.
